extracted.intended_audience: artists, art-critics, and students of art/theory
extracted.subtask_short: art criticism and judgement of paintings
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical framework for evaluating paintings and defining greatness in art; distinguishes technical execution (language) from intellectual content (thought) and classifies the sources of artistic pleasure into five kinds. Offers methodological guidance for critics on how to form and defend judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's method: prolonged doubt and accompanying demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Every one proposing to undertake criticism must strictly examine, with prolonged doubt and severe trial, every opinion contrary to received verdicts, and advance nothing which does not, at least in his own conviction, rest on surer ground than mere feeling or taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance nothing without accompanying demonstration; such demonstration 'can only be met on its own grounds, and can in no way be borne down or affected by mere authority of great names.' Criticism is useless when terms or grounds are ambiguous; avoid jargon that 'means everything, and nothing is expressed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not lump historical and landscape painters as equivalent 'old masters'
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought not to class the historical painters of the fifteenth, and landscape painters of the seventeenth, centuries, together under the general title of 'old masters,' as if they possessed anything like corresponding rank in their respective walks of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the principles on which historical and landscape painters worked are 'totally opposed'; compare like with like and, where necessary, consider certain artists (e.g., Poussin) apart because of separate character.

rubrics_metrics.name: State clear principles for right judgment of art
rubrics_metrics.description: All right judgment of art must be founded on clearly stated principles; criticism is useless when the terms or grounds of it are in any degree ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should study introductory principles carefully; avoid connoisseur jargon. Clarity of terms is essential so criticism can be understood and debated on its own grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between painter's intellectual power and technical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish those excellences in the painter which belong to him as such, and those which belong to him in common with all men of intellect; this distinction determines sound judgment of the rank of the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to whether qualities are evidence of intellectual power (thought, conception) or mere technical proficiency; failure to attend leads to coxcombry and error in criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting is a language; execution is not the test of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting, with all its technicalities, is nothing but a noble and expressive language, invaluable as the vehicle of thought, but by itself nothing; the greatness of a painter depends on what is represented and said, not on the mode of representing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical mastery (precision, force in 'language of lines') is necessary but not decisive; like grammar vs poetry, mastery of language doesn't make one a great artist unless substantial ideas are conveyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness depends on thought/images conveyed, not ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: A great painter should be judged by the character of the images or thoughts which his language conveys; the picture which has the nobler and more numerous ideas is a greater and better picture than one with finer execution but less thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank and praise pictures chiefly for thought; consider decorative excellence (color, finish) as inferior and unable to outweigh even small losses of idea. 'Nothing but thought can pay for thought.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish decorative (ornamental) from expressive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between what is ornamental in language and what is expressive; that part necessary to convey the thought is respectable, but decorative parts are like frame or varnish and little to do with intrinsic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: in painting mere beauty of language can be very attractive and mislead judges into thinking it equals thought; avoid promoting 'ornamental writing-masters' to authorship because of prettiness of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of great art: conveys greatest number of the greatest ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest picture is that which conveys to the mind of the spectator the greatest number of the greatest ideas; an idea is great in proportion as it is received by a higher faculty of the mind and more fully exercises and exalts that faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is meant to be wide enough to include all aims of art (to please, to teach, to imitate, to create); use it as the principal test of artistic greatness and to derive the rank of artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a great artist
rubrics_metrics.description: He is the greatest artist who has embodied, in the sum of his works, the greatest number of the greatest ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the artist by the cumulative ideas embodied across works, not merely by technical skill or isolated effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sources of pleasure into five kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: All sources of pleasure or other good from works of art may be referred to five heads: I. Ideas of Power; II. Ideas of Imitation; III. Ideas of Truth; IV. Ideas of Beauty; V. Ideas of Relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five categories as a framework to analyse what a work of art conveys and which kinds of ideas it supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of Power: perception of the powers exerted by the artist
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of Power are the simple perception or conception of the mental or bodily powers by which the work has been produced; according to the dignity and degree of the power perceived is the dignity of the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ideas excite veneration and desire of exertion; they range from perception of manual labor (e.g., carved paddle) to exalted intellect; evidence of labor, dexterity, ingenuity, judgment multiply the sensation of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence defined by difficulty/power expended ('Power is never wasted')
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever difficulty has been overcome there is excellence; a thing is 'excellent' in proportion to the great power required for its production — 'Power is never wasted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excellence depends on the difficulty of production alone (separate from usefulness or beauty); to prove excellence, show the difficulty overcome. Beware blaming artists for technical display unless they have preferred inferior difficulties to great ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of excellence requires practice and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of perceiving what powers are required for the production of a thing is the faculty of perceiving excellence, and this faculty demands practice; without practice and knowledge one cannot estimate such powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even cultivated taste may appreciate beauty or truth, but only the practiced artist can detect 'excellence' (e.g., Titian's flesh-tint) because it demands personal measurement of toil and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in conquering difficulties is legitimate but must aim at great difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a right, ennobling pleasure in encountering and conquering opposition; but the artist is blamed when he seeks to show skill in overcoming technical or inferior difficulties rather than in reaching a great end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer great difficulties to mere technical feats; simplicity may be harder than complication, and sacrificing skill at the proper moment is often the higher achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of Imitation: definition as pleasurable deception
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'idea of imitation' is the pleasure felt when anything looks like what it is not — a resemblance nearly to deceive, producing pleasurable surprise similar to juggling; two things are requisite: resemblance nearly to deceive, and some means of proving the deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation is strongest where senses contradict (e.g., eye says round, finger says flat) — hence painting and wax-work excel in this. The pleasure depends on perfection of resemblance and the evidence that it is a deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is contemptible as an artistic source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of imitation are the most contemptible which can be received from art: they preclude high or noble emotion, are associated with mean and paltry subjects (it is impossible to imitate anything really great), and are relatively easy to achieve compared to ideas of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because imitation requires little ingenuity beyond a true eye and steady hand, it lacks associated ideas of power; its pleasures are akin to sensual surprise and cannot coexist with the loftier moral or intellectual effects of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions where imitation-pleasure is not contemptible (diorama/stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The remarks on imitation do not apply to the art of the Diorama or the stage, where the pleasure is not dependent on deception but is the same as from nature herself and can be noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that theatrical and dioramic presentation can produce noble pleasure similar to experiencing nature; in such cases imitation is not merely juggler-like trickery.
